catalog_quote: Like is the case with most of the African languages south of the Sahara, Lunyole is a tonal language. The language exhibits register tone, rather than contour tone. ... The language has basically a two-tone system where each vowel may be high or low tone. Syllables with two moras, i.e. those with long vowels and pre-nasalized consonants, may on rare occasions bear a rising or falling tone. Lunyole exhibits a very light functional load with rare tonal lexical pairs and grammatical tone. ... [9.1.1] Lunyole nouns exhibit a two-tone system and four common tone patterns: HH, HL, LH, and LL. However, in some few cases a rising or falling tone may occur . These four patterns are realized on the noun with its prefix. The prefix itself may take a H, L, LH or HL tone. There is no residual floating tone in Lunyole. ... new_statements.quote: Like is the case with most of the African languages south of the Sahara, Lunyole is a tonal language. The language exhibits register tone, rather than contour tone. [...] The language has basically a two-tone system where each vowel may be high or low tone. Syllables with two moras, i.e. those with long vowels and pre-nasalized consonants, may on rare occasions bear a rising or falling tone. Lunyole exhibits a very light functional load with rare tonal lexical pairs and grammatical tone. [...] (9.4) It appears there is a free distribution of tone – both the high and low tone may occur on any syllable in a word whether on the first or last syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Lunyole is described purely as a two-level (H/L) register-tone language with lexical and grammatical tone contrasts of low functional load; H and L are positionally free within the word. The source (and every other opened description: Wicks 2006, Namulemu 2014, Marlo et al. 2017) makes no statement at all about word stress, accent, or a fixed prominence position.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal notes only: contour (rising/falling) tones are rare and confined to bimoraic syllables; vowels are automatically long before NC and after Cw/Cy (sec. 6.1.2.3); tone is not marked in the orthography.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone in citation forms (nouns with augment+prefix, infinitives); Marlo et al. 2017 add phrase-level verb-tone melodies for the Lower Nyole variety. No stress domain is described anywhere.
new_statements.identity_note: Namulemu 2006, Wicks 2006 and Namulemu 2014 describe Upper Nyole / Lunyole proper (Butaleja District, mainly the Lumenya prestige dialect) = nyol1238 [nuj]. Marlo et al. 2017 describe 'Lower Nyole', a moribund resettlement variety of the same JE35 language spoken in Mayuge District, south Busoga (no separate glottocode; not to be confused with Kenyan Nyore/Olunyole JE33, nyor1246).

sources.note: Nothing: the word 'stress'/'accent' does not occur. Sec. 9 'Tone' (pp. 32-37): Lunyole is a tonal (register-tone) language with a two-tone H/L system, rare contours on bimoraic syllables, light functional load; sec. 9.4: H and L may occur on any syllable of the word. No statement on word stress or prominence.
